etymology: Renders the Hebrew hesed, denoting steadfast, loyal, covenant-keeping love and mercy; the LORD's faithful kindness that does not fail.
biblical_def: Covenant love is the steadfast, unbreakable affection of the LORD toward His people, a love rooted not in their loveliness but in His own free purpose and sworn covenant. The Hebrew hesed binds together love, mercy, loyalty, and faithfulness, so that the LORD loves with a love that keeps its word. Because the new covenant rests upon the finished work of Christ and the eternal election of the Father, this love is the immovable ground of the believer's security. Jeremiah cries in the ashes of Jerusalem that the LORD's mercies are new every morning and His faithfulness is great, for it is of His covenant love that we are not consumed. The Psalmist repeats six and twenty times that His mercy endures for ever, anchoring all creation and all redemption in this enduring kindness. Such love is not sentiment but covenant fidelity—the LORD will be a God to His people and to their seed, and none shall pluck them from His hand. The believer does not earn this love, nor can he forfeit it, for the Son has purchased His bride and the Spirit seals her unto the day of redemption. Here the saint rests in storm and sin alike: not upon the strength of his own grasp, but upon the everlasting arms of a God whose love is as faithful as His throne is eternal. This is the fountain of assurance and the spring of all obedience.
webster_summary: Steadfast covenant-keeping love; the loyal mercy and faithfulness of God toward His people.
webster_full: COVENANT LOVE, noun phrase. Renders the Hebrew hesed, steadfast loyal love and mercy bound to covenant fidelity.
The loyal kindness of God whereby He keeps the promises He has sworn to His people.
A love that springs from God's free purpose rather than from anything in the object loved.
As Lamentations 3:22 declares, "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not."
The settled ground of a believer's assurance, since this love neither began nor ends with man's deserving.
scriptures: Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
Lam 3:23
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Jer 31:3
The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.
corruption_summary: The age sentimentalizes God's love into unconditional approval untethered from covenant, holiness, or judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern world clings to the word love while stripping it of covenant. God's love is recast as a boundless affirmation that asks nothing, judges nothing, and changes no one—a divine indulgence that smiles upon every path and condition. But the LORD's hesed is covenant love, sworn within a covenant that has stipulations, a Mediator, and a holy God at its center. It is not the abolition of His justice but the very thing that satisfied His justice at the cross.

To recover the truth we must hold love and covenant together as Scripture does. The LORD loves His people with an everlasting love, but He loves them in Christ, through the blood of the covenant, and unto holiness. This love is steadfast precisely because it is anchored in His unchanging purpose and not in the shifting affections of men. Such a doctrine humbles the proud, comforts the broken, and binds the saint to grateful obedience rather than presumptuous license.
roots_summary: Covenant love springs from God's eternal purpose and is displayed in His faithful dealings across redemptive history.
roots_lines: The Hebrew hesed joins love, mercy, loyalty, and faithfulness in one covenant word.
It flows from God's free election, not from any worth in the people loved.
It is sworn within covenant and so cannot be broken by human failure.
It is supremely displayed at the cross, where mercy and justice meet.
It is the immovable ground of the believer's assurance and perseverance.
usage: Believers rest their assurance not on their feeble grasp but on the covenant love that holds them fast.
Preachers proclaim that the LORD's mercies are new every morning to comfort the weary saint.
The doctrine guards the church against both legal despair and presumptuous license.

etymology: From the Hebrew 'oth and Greek sphragis (seal); a visible token God appoints to mark, confirm, and seal His covenant promise.
biblical_def: A covenant sign is a visible token that God Himself appoints to mark, confirm, and seal the promises of His covenant, distinguishing the sign from the thing it signifies. To Noah He gave the rainbow that He would no more destroy the earth by flood; to Abraham He gave circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith; to Israel He gave the Passover, that the destroying angel might pass over the blood-marked door. These signs neither create nor contain the grace they point to, yet they are not empty, for God binds His word to them and pledges Himself in them. Under the new covenant the signs are baptism and the Lord's Supper, the one sealing union with Christ in His death and resurrection, the other showing forth His broken body and shed blood till He come. The Reformed faith ever distinguishes the sign from the thing signified: the water is not the washing of the soul, nor the bread the very body, yet the believing recipient truly receives Christ and all His benefits by faith through the Spirit. Thus the sacraments are signs and seals of the covenant of grace, confirming the promise to the eye as the Word confirms it to the ear. They strengthen weak faith, mark the visible people of God, and direct the heart away from the token to the Christ it represents.
webster_summary: A visible token God appoints to mark and seal His covenant, distinct from the grace it signifies.
webster_full: COVENANT SIGN, noun phrase. From the Hebrew 'oth and Greek sphragis, a visible seal God appoints to confirm His covenant.
A token divinely instituted, such as the rainbow, circumcision, the Passover, baptism, and the Lord's Supper.
The sign is ever distinguished from the thing signified, yet sacramentally united to it by God's word.
Of Abraham it is written in Romans 4:11 that he "received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith."
A means whereby God confirms His promise to the eye, strengthening the faith of His people.
scriptures: Rom 4:11
And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised:
Gen 9:13
I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
And ye shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a token of the covenant betwixt me and you.
And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you.
corruption_summary: Error gathers at both extremes—some make the sign empty ritual, others make it confer the grace it merely signifies.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors crowd around the covenant sign. The one empties it of meaning, treating baptism and the Supper as bare memorials or social customs with no abiding pledge of God. The other collapses the sign into the thing signified, so that the water is thought to wash the soul and the bread to become the very flesh of Christ—a confusion the Reformed faith firmly resists in distinguishing the seal from that which it seals.

To recover the truth we must hold the sign and the thing signified together yet distinct, as Scripture does. God truly pledges Himself in the appointed token, and the believing soul truly receives Christ by faith through the Spirit, yet the grace is not bound within the element nor conferred apart from faith. So the rainbow preached mercy, circumcision sealed righteousness by faith, and baptism and the Supper confirm the covenant of grace to the eye, ever pointing beyond themselves to Christ.
roots_summary: Covenant signs run through redemptive history as God's appointed seals of His sworn promise.
roots_lines: God Himself institutes the sign; man may not invent or alter it.
The sign is distinguished from the thing signified, yet united to it by God's word.
The rainbow, circumcision, and Passover were the chief signs under the old covenant.
Baptism and the Lord's Supper are the signs and seals of the new covenant.
The signs confirm the promise to the eye and direct faith to Christ alone.
usage: The church administers the covenant signs as God appointed them, neither despising nor over-valuing the elements.
Pastors teach the people to look through the sign to the Christ it seals.
The believer's faith is strengthened as the promise is confirmed to the eye in baptism and the Supper.

etymology: From the Hebrew da'ath (intimate experiential knowing) and Greek gnōsis; not bare information but the heart's saving apprehension of God.
biblical_def: The knowledge of God is the soul's saving apprehension of the living God as He has revealed Himself in His Word and supremely in Christ. It is no bare intellectual grasp of doctrine, though it is never less than truth rightly understood, but a knowing that grips the heart, bows the will, and transforms the life. Our Lord defines life eternal itself as this knowledge: that men should know the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom He hath sent. The prophet Jeremiah forbids the wise to glory in wisdom or the mighty in might, that he who glories may glory in this—that he understands and knows the LORD who exercises lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness in the earth. Such knowledge is the gift of regeneration, for the natural man receives not the things of the Spirit, neither can he know them. It begins where the Spirit opens blind eyes, grows as the believer beholds the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, and ripens into that perfect knowing when faith gives way to sight. It is therefore both doctrinal and experiential, comprising right thoughts of God and a heart drawn out in love, fear, and trust toward Him. This knowledge humbles the proud, comforts the afflicted, and conforms the saint to the image of the One whom he knows, so that to grow in grace is to grow in the knowledge of God Himself.
webster_summary: The soul's saving apprehension of God in Christ; not mere information but a heart-transforming knowing.
webster_full: KNOWLEDGE OF GOD, noun phrase. From the Hebrew da'ath and Greek gnōsis, an intimate experiential knowing, not bare information.
The saving apprehension of the true God as revealed in His Word and in Christ.
A knowing that engages the mind, bows the will, and warms the affections toward God.
Our Lord declares in John 17:3, "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."
The gift of the regenerating Spirit, who alone opens blind eyes to behold God's glory.
scriptures: Joh 17:3
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
Jer 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
Hos 6:3
Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD: his going forth is prepared as the morning;
corruption_summary: The knowledge of God is reduced either to cold doctrine or to mystical feeling untethered from revealed truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions assail the knowledge of God. The one shrinks it to mere intellectual assent—a stockpile of correct propositions held without love, fear, or trust, the very thing devils possess while they tremble. The other dissolves it into formless feeling and private spirituality, an inner experience cut loose from the God who has spoken, so that men profess to know a deity of their own imagining rather than the LORD of Scripture.

To recover the truth we must bind knowing and being known together as Scripture does. True knowledge of God is grounded in His self-revelation, apprehended by a regenerate heart, and proved by love and obedience. It is neither dry orthodoxy nor untethered mysticism, but the saving sight of God's glory in the face of Christ, given by the Spirit, that bows the soul in worship and conforms it to the image of the One it knows.
roots_summary: Saving knowledge of God begins in regeneration, grows through the Word, and ripens unto glory.
roots_lines: God can be truly known only as He reveals Himself in His Word and in Christ.
The natural man cannot know God savingly until the Spirit opens his blind eyes.
This knowledge engages the whole man—mind, will, and affections together.
It grows as the believer beholds the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
It is consummated when faith yields to sight and the saint knows even as he is known.
usage: The Christian counts all things loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord.
Preachers labor that the people might know God truly and not merely know about Him.
Growth in grace is measured by growth in the saving knowledge of God.

etymology: From the Hebrew mul (to circumcise) applied figuratively to the heart; the inward cutting away of sin that the outward sign foreshadowed.
biblical_def: Circumcision of the heart is the inward, spiritual work of regeneration whereby God cuts away the corruption and hardness of the soul, fulfilling what the outward sign in the flesh could only foreshadow. Moses promised that the LORD would circumcise the heart of His people to love Him with all the heart and soul, that they might live. Paul declares that he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not of men but of God. Thus the true seed of Abraham are those whose hearts God has renewed, not merely those who bear the badge in the body. In Colossians the apostle joins this circumcision made without hands to union with Christ, the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ, accomplished in regeneration and signified in baptism. This work is monergistic: God alone wields the knife, for the natural man cannot soften his own stony heart. It is the removal of the foreskin of unbelief, the implanting of a new principle of life and love, and the making of a willing people who delight in the law of God after the inward man. Here the shadow gives way to substance: the sign in the flesh pointed all along to this saving renewal of the heart by the Spirit of God.
webster_summary: The inward work of regeneration that cuts away sin's corruption, fulfilling what outward circumcision foreshadowed.
webster_full: CIRCUMCISION OF THE HEART, noun phrase. From the Hebrew mul, to circumcise, applied figuratively to the renewing of the inner man.
The inward spiritual renewal of regeneration, of which fleshly circumcision was the outward sign.
A work wrought by God alone, who cuts away the hardness and corruption of the heart.
Moses foretells in Deuteronomy 30:6 that "the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart."
Paul teaches that true circumcision is "that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter."
scriptures: Deu 30:6
And the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live.
Rom 2:29
But he is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, and not in the letter; whose praise is not of men, but of God.
Col 2:11
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh by the circumcision of Christ:
Jer 4:4
Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem:
corruption_summary: Men trust the outward badge or rite while the heart remains uncircumcised and unrenewed.
corruption_paragraphs: The perennial error is to rest in the outward sign while the inward reality is wholly lacking. Israel boasted in circumcised flesh while their hearts remained hard and rebellious; so men today may trust in baptism, church membership, or religious heritage while the soul has never been renewed by the Spirit. The sign without the substance saves no one, for God looks upon the heart and is not deceived by the badge in the body.

To recover the truth we must press home that God requires a circumcised heart, and that He alone can give it. The outward sign was never meant to stand alone but to point to the inward cutting away of sin that comes by regeneration. Therefore men must not rest in any rite but cry to God for the new heart He has promised, knowing that true religion is inward, spiritual, and wrought by the Spirit of the living God.
roots_summary: The inward circumcision is the reality long foreshadowed by the outward sign in the flesh.
roots_lines: The outward circumcision of the flesh signified an inward renewal of the heart.
God Himself promised to circumcise the heart of His people unto love and life.
Paul locates true circumcision in the heart, by the Spirit, not in the letter.
Colossians joins this circumcision without hands to union with Christ in regeneration.
The work is monergistic: God alone cuts away the hardness of the soul.
usage: The preacher warns hearers not to rest in the outward sign while the heart remains unrenewed.
Believers thank God for the circumcision made without hands wrought in their regeneration.
The doctrine distinguishes the visible badge from the saving reality it signified.

etymology: From the Greek loutron palingenesias, the laver or washing of new birth; the Spirit's cleansing renewal of the soul in regeneration.
biblical_def: The washing of regeneration is the cleansing, renewing work of the Holy Spirit whereby a dead sinner is born again and made a new creature in Christ. Paul declares that not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy God saved us, by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost. The washing here is not the water of baptism conferring grace, but the inward purification of the soul wrought by the Spirit, of which baptism is the outward sign and seal. This is the new birth the Lord pressed upon Nicodemus—that a man must be born of water and of the Spirit, the water signifying that very Spirit's cleansing of the heart. It is a sovereign and monergistic act: the sinner is passive, being acted upon, not cooperating, for the dead cannot raise themselves. By this washing the old defilement is purged, a new principle of life is implanted, and the will is renewed to love and follow God. It is joined inseparably to justification, for those whom the Spirit washes are also reckoned righteous in Christ, yet it is distinct, being the inward change of nature rather than the change of standing. The Reformed faith guards this doctrine jealously against the error that makes the rite itself regenerate the soul, insisting rather that the Spirit blows where He lists, granting new birth to whom He will, and that the outward sign profits only where the inward grace is given.
webster_summary: The Spirit's cleansing renewal of the soul in the new birth, signified—but not effected—by baptism.
webster_full: WASHING OF REGENERATION, noun phrase. From the Greek loutron palingenesias, the laver or washing of new birth.
The inward cleansing and renewing of the soul wrought by the Holy Spirit in regeneration.
The outward water of baptism signifies and seals this washing but does not itself confer it.
Paul writes in Titus 3:5 that God "saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost."
A sovereign and monergistic work in which the sinner is passive and the Spirit alone gives life.
scriptures: Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Joh 3:5
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
Then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
corruption_summary: The grave error is baptismal regeneration—teaching that the water of the rite itself washes away sin and confers the new birth.
corruption_paragraphs: The most serious corruption of this text is the doctrine of baptismal regeneration, taught by Rome and other sacramentalists, which holds that the new birth is conferred by the application of baptismal water itself, so that the rite ex opere operato washes away original sin and makes the recipient a child of God. This confuses the sign with the thing signified and makes the salvation of the soul hang upon a ceremony rather than upon the sovereign work of the Spirit. Scripture will not bear it: Simon Magus was baptized yet remained in the gall of bitterness, and Paul ascribes salvation to God's mercy and the renewing of the Holy Ghost, not to the bare element.

To recover the truth we must distinguish sharply between the outward washing of water and the inward washing of the Spirit. Baptism is the sign and seal of regeneration, a precious ordinance to be honored, but it is not regeneration itself. The Spirit gives the new birth sovereignly, to whom He will, and the rite profits only where He has already wrought, or shall work, the inward grace. So we honor baptism without idolizing it, and we ground salvation where God grounds it—in His mercy and the renewing of the Holy Ghost.
roots_summary: The washing of regeneration is the Spirit's inward cleansing, distinct from yet signified by baptism.
roots_lines: The washing is the Spirit's inward renewal, not the outward water of the rite.
It is a sovereign, monergistic act in which the dead sinner is wholly passive.
Ezekiel foretold this cleansing under the figure of clean water sprinkled by God.
Baptism signifies and seals the washing but does not confer it.
The doctrine stands against baptismal regeneration, grounding new birth in the Spirit alone.
usage: The believer rejoices that God saved him by the washing of regeneration and not by his own works.
Pastors teach that the water of baptism signifies, but does not effect, the new birth.
The doctrine guards the church against trusting a rite in place of the Spirit's renewing work.

etymology: From the Greek loutron tou hudatos en rhēmati in Ephesians 5:26, the washing of water by the word; the Word as the Spirit's cleansing instrument.
biblical_def: The water of the word is the Holy Scripture as the instrument by which Christ sanctifies and cleanses His church. Paul writes that Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, that He might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that He might present it to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle. The figure draws on the cleansing power of water, but the apostle names the means plainly: it is the word that washes. As the body is made clean by water, so the soul is purified by the truth of God applied by the Spirit. Our Lord prayed for His own, sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth; and He told His disciples, now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you. Thus sanctification is no mystical process apart from Scripture, nor a mere outward conformity, but the progressive cleansing of the soul as the Word of God dwells richly within and the Spirit wields it against indwelling sin. The Word convicts, instructs, reproves, and renews; it washes away the defilement of error and corruption; it conforms the believer to the image of Christ. This cleansing is ongoing, the daily work of grace in the Christian life, for the church is being sanctified now and shall be presented glorious at the last. Here is the great means God has appointed: His own Word, read, preached, and believed, washing the bride He purchased with His blood.
webster_summary: The Scripture as Christ's appointed means of sanctifying and cleansing His church.
webster_full: WATER OF THE WORD, noun phrase. From the Greek loutron tou hudatos en rhēmati, the washing of water by the word.
The Holy Scripture viewed as the cleansing instrument by which Christ sanctifies His people.
A figure drawn from water's cleansing power, applied to the purifying truth of God.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:26 that Christ sanctifies the church, "cleansing it with the washing of water by the word."
The ordinary means of progressive sanctification, the Word wielded by the Spirit against indwelling sin.
scriptures: Eph 5:26
That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word,
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
Joh 15:3
Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.
Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.
corruption_summary: Sanctification is sought in inner feeling, technique, or experience while the cleansing Word is neglected.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the practical neglect of the Word as the means of sanctification is everywhere. Many seek holiness through inner feeling, programs, or private spiritual experiences while the appointed laver—the Scripture itself—lies unopened and unread. The result is a religion of sentiment that produces no cleansing, for it bypasses the very instrument Christ has ordained to wash His church.

To recover the truth we must return to the water of the word as the primary means of grace. Christ sanctifies His bride by the washing of His Word, applied by the Spirit, and there is no cleansing of the soul that does not flow through Scripture read, preached, sung, and obeyed. Therefore the believer who would grow in holiness must dwell in the Word, letting it convict, reprove, instruct, and renew, until he is conformed to the image of the Christ who gave Himself for the church.
roots_summary: The Word is Christ's appointed instrument for cleansing and sanctifying His blood-bought church.
roots_lines: Christ sanctifies the church by the washing of water by the word.
The figure of water signifies the cleansing power of God's truth.
Our Lord prayed that His people be sanctified through the truth of the Word.
Sanctification is progressive, the ongoing cleansing of the soul by Scripture.
The Spirit wields the Word against indwelling sin to conform the saint to Christ.
usage: The believer feeds daily on the water of the word that he may be cleansed and sanctified.
Pastors preach the Word knowing it is Christ's appointed means of washing the church.
Growth in holiness is sought through Scripture, not through feeling apart from it.

etymology: From the Greek anexichniaston ploutos, riches that cannot be traced out or fully explored; the inexhaustible fulness of Christ.
biblical_def: The unsearchable riches of Christ are the boundless, inexhaustible treasures of grace, wisdom, and glory that are stored up in the Lord Jesus and freely preached to sinners. Paul, esteeming himself less than the least of all saints, counted it grace given to him to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ—riches so vast that they cannot be traced out, so deep that no creature can fathom them, so full that they meet every want of the soul forever. In Christ are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily; of His fulness have all we received, and grace for grace. These riches comprise His person and His work: His perfect righteousness imputed to the believer, His blood that cleanses from all sin, His Spirit that renews and seals, His intercession that never fails, and the inheritance incorruptible reserved in heaven. They are unsearchable not because they are hidden from faith but because they exceed all measure; the saint may draw forever and never drain the fountain. To preach Christ is therefore to set forth this infinite treasure to bankrupt sinners, that they might come and buy without money and without price. And to grow in grace is to enter ever more deeply into these riches, beholding new wonders of His glory, finding fresh supplies for every need, until the day when faith gives way to sight and the redeemed shall explore forever the unsearchable fulness of their Lord.
webster_summary: The boundless, inexhaustible treasures of grace and glory stored up in Christ and preached to sinners.
webster_full: UNSEARCHABLE RICHES OF CHRIST, noun phrase. From the Greek anexichniaston ploutos, riches that cannot be traced out or fully explored.
The boundless treasures of grace, wisdom, and glory that dwell in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Riches so vast and deep that no creature can fathom or exhaust them.
Paul declares in Ephesians 3:8 that grace was given him "to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ."
The infinite fulness from which every believer receives grace for grace.
scriptures: Eph 3:8
Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
Joh 1:16
And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.
Col 1:19
For it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell;
corruption_summary: Christ's fulness is diminished into one teacher among many or reduced to mere earthly benefit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the riches of Christ are commonly diminished. Some shrink Him to a wise teacher or moral example, one voice among many, robbing Him of the infinite fulness Scripture ascribes to Him. Others, in a prosperity spirit, reduce His riches to earthly health and wealth, mistaking the gift of Himself for a means to temporal gain, when the true treasure is Christ and all His saving benefits.

To recover the truth we must preach Christ as the inexhaustible treasure He is—in whom dwells all the fulness of the Godhead, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom, and from whose fulness the saint receives grace upon grace. These riches are spiritual and eternal: righteousness, reconciliation, adoption, sanctification, and glory. To know Him is to possess all things, and the labor of the Christian life is to explore forever a fulness that can never be drained.
roots_summary: The riches of Christ are infinite, spiritual, and inexhaustible, preached freely to bankrupt sinners.
roots_lines: The Greek names riches that cannot be traced out or fully explored.
All the fulness of the Godhead and the treasures of wisdom dwell in Christ.
These riches comprise His person and His whole saving work.
They are freely preached to sinners who have nothing with which to buy.
The believer draws upon them forever and never drains the fountain.
usage: The preacher sets forth the unsearchable riches of Christ to needy and bankrupt sinners.
The believer finds in Christ a fulness that supplies every want of the soul.
Growth in grace is the ever-deepening exploration of these inexhaustible riches.

etymology: From the Greek auxanō (to grow, increase) joined with charis (grace); the believer's progressive increase in grace and knowledge.
biblical_def: Growing in grace is the believer's progressive increase in holiness, faith, and the knowledge of Christ throughout the whole course of the Christian life. Peter closes his epistle with the command, grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ—a charge that joins inward growth to a deepening apprehension of Christ Himself. This growth is the fruit of regeneration and the work of sanctification: having been born again by the incorruptible seed of the Word, the believer desires the sincere milk of the Word that he may grow thereby. It is gradual and progressive, not instantaneous; the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day. Yet it is real, for God who began the good work will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. The means are appointed: the Word, prayer, the sacraments, fellowship, and the providential discipline of God, all wielded by the Spirit to mortify sin and quicken graces. Such growth is not the believer's own achievement but the operation of grace within him, even as he works out his salvation with fear and trembling because God works in him both to will and to do. The marks of it are increasing humility, deepening love, sharper hatred of sin, and a fuller delight in Christ. Thus the saint, though never sinless in this life, is ever being conformed more closely to the image of his Lord until grace is consummated in glory.
webster_summary: The believer's progressive increase in grace, holiness, and the knowledge of Christ.
webster_full: GROWING IN GRACE, verbal phrase. From the Greek auxanō, to grow or increase, joined with charis, grace.
The progressive increase of the believer in holiness, faith, and the knowledge of Christ.
The ongoing fruit of regeneration and the work of sanctification in the soul.
Peter commands in 2 Peter 3:18, "But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ."
A gradual and lifelong work, real yet never complete until consummated in glory.
scriptures: But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
Pro 4:18
But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
Phi 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Sanctification is recast as self-improvement, instant perfection, or mere positive change apart from grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet growing in grace is often distorted within the church. Some make it a program of self-help and self-improvement, a matter of human effort and technique rather than the work of the Spirit. Others swing to perfectionism, claiming a sudden entire sanctification that Scripture nowhere promises in this life, while still others deny progressive growth altogether, presuming upon grace while remaining content in sin.

To recover the truth we must hold that growth in grace is genuine, gradual, and wrought by God. The believer truly increases in holiness and the knowledge of Christ, yet this increase is the operation of grace within him, even as he diligently uses the means God has appointed. He works out his salvation because God works in him to will and to do. So the Christian neither despairs at slow progress nor presumes upon a perfection not yet given, but presses on, confident that He who began the good work will complete it in glory.
roots_summary: Growing in grace is the progressive, Spirit-wrought increase of the regenerate soul toward Christ.
roots_lines: Growth in grace flows from regeneration and is the work of sanctification.
It is progressive and lifelong, not instantaneous or perfected in this life.
It is wrought by God through appointed means: Word, prayer, sacraments, and providence.
The believer labors in it because God works in him both to will and to do.
Its marks are deeper humility, love, hatred of sin, and delight in Christ.
usage: The believer uses the means of grace diligently that he may grow thereby.
Pastors call the saints to grow in grace and in the knowledge of their Lord.
Slow progress drives the Christian to grace rather than to despair.

etymology: From the Greek plērophoria pisteos, full conviction or settled certainty of faith; the believer's confident drawing near to God.
biblical_def: The full assurance of faith is the settled, well-grounded confidence whereby the believer draws near to God through Christ, resting upon the sufficiency of His blood and intercession. The writer to the Hebrews exhorts, let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. Paul desires that the saints' hearts be comforted, being knit together in love, unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ. This assurance is not presumption, nor a fleeting feeling, but a confidence built upon the promises of God, the finished work of Christ, and the inward witness of the Spirit. It rests first upon the objective ground of the gospel—Christ crucified, risen, and pleading—and is confirmed by the subjective evidences of grace within and the testimony of the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are the children of God. Such assurance does not belong to the essence of saving faith, so that a true believer may walk for a season without it; yet it is the privilege and proper fruit of faith, to be diligently sought through the means of grace. It produces holy boldness before the throne, peace amid trial, and a heart enlarged for obedience and worship. The full assurance of faith is therefore the settled rest of the soul upon Christ, a confidence that emboldens the saint to draw near, knowing he is accepted in the Beloved.
webster_summary: The settled confidence whereby the believer draws near to God, resting on Christ's finished work.
webster_full: FULL ASSURANCE OF FAITH, noun phrase. From the Greek plērophoria pisteos, full conviction or settled certainty of faith.
The well-grounded confidence of the believer in drawing near to God through Christ.
Built upon the promises of God, the finished work of Christ, and the witness of the Spirit.
Hebrews 10:22 exhorts, "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience."
A privilege and fruit of faith, distinct from its essence, to be diligently sought.
scriptures: Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
Col 2:2

That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ;
Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.
corruption_summary: Assurance is reduced to mere feeling, or denied to believers, or presumed upon by the unregenerate.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet assurance is variously corrupted within the church. Some reduce it to a passing emotional feeling, so that confidence rises and falls with the moods of the soul. Others deny that any believer may be assured at all, leaving the saints in perpetual doubt and robbing them of their birthright of peace. And many among the unregenerate presume upon a false assurance, resting in a bare profession while their lives betray no grace.

To recover the truth we must ground assurance where Scripture grounds it—upon the promises of God, the finished work of Christ, and the witness of the Spirit, confirmed by the evidences of grace within. It is not the essence of faith, so a true believer may lack it for a season; yet it is the proper fruit of faith, to be sought through the diligent use of the means of grace. So the saint examines himself, but rests his confidence not on himself but on Christ, drawing near with boldness to the throne of grace.
roots_summary: Full assurance rests on God's promises, Christ's work, and the Spirit's witness, confirmed by grace within.
roots_lines: Assurance is a settled confidence, not a fleeting feeling or presumption.
Its objective ground is the gospel: Christ crucified, risen, and interceding.
Its subjective confirmation is the Spirit's witness and the evidences of grace.
It is not the essence of faith, so a believer may lack it for a season.
It is the privilege of faith, to be sought through the means of grace.
usage: The believer draws near to the throne of grace in the full assurance of faith.
Pastors press the saints to seek assurance through the diligent use of the means of grace.
True assurance produces boldness, peace, and an enlarged heart for obedience.

etymology: From the Greek agōnizou ton kalon agōna, to contend the noble contest, drawn from the athletic and military arena; the warfare of faith.
biblical_def: To fight the good fight is to wage the lifelong warfare of faith, contending against sin, the world, and the devil, and persevering unto the end in the strength that God supplies. Paul charges Timothy, fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called; and at the close of his own course he testifies, I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. The figure is drawn from both the wrestling-ground and the battlefield, for the Christian life is no idle ease but a strenuous and holy striving. The believer is a soldier of Jesus Christ, called to endure hardness, to put on the whole armour of God, and to war a good warfare. This conflict is real and unceasing: the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; principalities and powers assail the soul; and the world allures with its pleasures and threatens with its frowns. Yet the fight is good, for it is fought in a good cause, by good weapons that are mighty through God, for a glorious crown that fadeth not away. The believer does not fight in his own strength but is strengthened with might by the Spirit in the inner man, and is assured of final victory because Christ has already overcome. This warfare is inseparable from the perseverance of the saints, for those whom God has called He keeps, enabling them to endure unto the end and to lay hold on the eternal life to which they were called.
webster_summary: To wage the lifelong warfare of faith, persevering against sin and Satan unto the end.
webster_full: FIGHT THE GOOD FIGHT, verbal phrase. From the Greek agōnizou ton kalon agōna, to contend the noble contest.
The lifelong warfare of faith against sin, the world, and the devil.
A figure drawn from the athletic arena and the battlefield, denoting strenuous holy striving.
Paul charges in 1 Timothy 6:12, "Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called."
A conflict fought in God's strength and crowned with certain victory through Christ.
scriptures: Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: The warfare of faith is softened into ease and self-fulfillment, or twisted into mere human striving apart from grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the warfare of faith is widely softened within the church. Many recast the Christian life as a path of ease, comfort, and self-fulfillment, with no enemy to resist and no cross to bear. Others, swinging to the opposite error, make the fight a matter of mere human willpower and self-discipline, as though the believer overcame in his own strength rather than in the might that God supplies.

To recover the truth we must own the Christian life as a real and unceasing conflict, yet one waged in grace and assured of victory. The believer is a soldier called to endure hardness, to put on the whole armour of God, and to resist sin and Satan unto the end. But he fights in Christ's strength, with weapons mighty through God, persevering not by his own resolve but because God keeps those whom He has called. So the saint contends earnestly, knowing the crown is sure and the captain of his salvation has already overcome.
roots_summary: The good fight is the believer's lifelong, grace-empowered warfare ending in certain victory.
roots_lines: The Greek draws on both the wrestling-ground and the battlefield for its figure.
The Christian wars against the flesh, the world, and the devil.
The fight is good because of its cause, its weapons, and its crown.
The believer fights not in his own strength but in the might of the Spirit.
The warfare is inseparable from the perseverance of the saints unto the end.
usage: The Christian endures hardness as a good soldier, fighting the good fight of faith.
Pastors arm the saints with the whole armour of God for the warfare of faith.
The aged believer looks back with Paul and says he has fought a good fight.
